questions.prompt: A teammate adds a skill that deploys to production and sets `disable-model-invocation: true` on it. What does that skill cost you at startup, in a session where you never type its name?
options: Its full body loads, so Claude knows what the side effect is
Nothing — it is left out of the startup listing entirely and costs zero until invoked
Only its description loads, so Claude can warn you before you trigger it
It loads when Claude reads a file matching its `paths:` pattern
questions.explanation: `disable-model-invocation: true` removes the skill from the startup listing, so neither description nor body is in the window until you invoke it by name. Option A is backwards: the switch exists precisely to keep side-effecting skills out of context. Option C describes the *default* behavior (description only), which is the thing the switch turns off. Option D confuses a skill with a path-scoped rule; `paths:` governs automatic activation, not listing cost.

questions.prompt: You connect an MCP server that exposes forty tools. You brace for a huge jump in your startup context, but `/context` barely moves. What is the most likely explanation?
options: MCP servers never enter the context window
Only the tool names load at startup; the full schemas are deferred and fetched on demand by tool search
The server failed to connect, so nothing loaded
All forty schemas loaded, but `/context` rounds numbers below 1,000 tokens
questions.explanation: By default, MCP tool names are listed at startup so Claude knows what exists, while the much larger schemas are deferred and loaded on demand via tool search. Option A is too strong: names and, when a tool is used, its schema do enter the window. Option C is a symptom you would see as tools failing to appear, not as a quietly small context. Option D misreads `/context`, which shows the block cost; forty schemas would be a visible jump, not a rounding artifact.

questions.prompt: Your project has a rule at `.claude/rules/api-conventions.md` with `paths: src/api/**`. You start a fresh session and edit only `src/lib/util.ts`. What did that rule cost?
options: A standing charge, because all rules load at startup
Nothing — path-scoped rules load only when a matching file is read
Its full text, because rules are always loaded and never path-scoped
Only its name, because the listing loads every rule's filename
questions.explanation: A path-scoped rule loads when a file matching its `paths:` pattern is read, so a session that never touches `src/api/` never pays for it. Option A is the classic misconception this lesson exists to kill. Option C contradicts the `paths:` field, which is exactly what scopes it. Option D is close but wrong: the detail that loads is the rule's content on a match, not a name at startup — that is the difference between a rule and a skill listing.

questions.prompt: Your auto-memory file has grown to 900 lines of notes. Which part can you count on being in the window at a new session's start?
options: All 900 lines, because auto memory always loads in full
None of it, because auto memory is only read on demand
The first 200 lines or 25 KB, whichever comes first
Only the lines Claude wrote most recently, up to 200
questions.explanation: Auto memory loads at startup, but only the first 200 lines or 25 KB, whichever comes first. Option A is the trap: it feels like memory should be all-or-nothing, but it is capped. Option B is wrong in the other direction — it is a startup block, not an on-demand read. Option D invents a recency rule; the cap is positional (the start of the file), which is why what you put at the top matters.
